title: United States v. Mead Corp. (2001)
summary: An agency interpretation gets Chevron deference only when Congress delegated authority to the agency to make rules with the force of law and the agency issued the interpretation in the exercise of that authority; otherwise the interpretation gets Skidmore respect measured by its power to persuade.
notes: Supreme Court of the United States, 2001. Key line: "We hold that administrative implementation of a particular statutory provision qualifies for Chevron deference when it appears that Congress delegated authority to the agency generally to make rules carrying the force of law, and that the agency interpretation claiming deference was promulgated in the exercise of that authority." (Justice Souter)

sections.Parties: The petitioner is the United States, defending a tariff classification ruling issued by the Customs Service, a bureau of the Treasury Department, and the position of the Solicitor General that such rulings deserve Chevron deference. The respondent is the Mead Corporation, an importer of day planners, which had paid no duty on them for years and challenged a Headquarters ruling letter that reclassified them as dutiable bound diaries. Amici on Mead's side included Filofax, importers' associations, the Customs and International Trade Bar Association, and Professor Thomas Merrill, whose article Chevron's Domain the Court cited for the idea that Chevron should apply only where Congress would want it to apply.
sections.Material Facts: Under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule, 19 U.S.C. § 1500(b) directs Customs to fix classifications under Treasury regulations, and § 1502(a) authorizes procedures for binding rulings before goods enter. Under 19 CFR § 177.9, a ruling letter binds Customs only as to the addressee's transaction and warns other importers not to rely on it. Any of 46 port offices or Headquarters may issue one without notice and comment; 10,000 to 15,000 issue each year. Mead's day planners were three-ring binders holding schedule pages, addresses, and a calendar. Subheading 4820.10.20, "[d]iaries, notebooks and address books, bound," carried a 4.0% duty; subheading 4820.10.40, "[o]ther," was duty free. Customs treated the planners as "other" from 1989 until a January 1993 Headquarters letter called them bound diaries; after Mead protested, Headquarters issued a reasoned but unpublished letter reaching the same result, relying on a broad Oxford English Dictionary definition of "diary" and reading "bound" to include metal or plastic fittings.
sections.Procedural History: Customs rejected Mead's protest of the second Headquarters letter. Mead sued in the Court of International Trade, which granted the Government summary judgment, adopting Customs's reasoning without discussing deference, 17 F. Supp. 2d 1004 (1998). While Mead's appeal was pending, the Supreme Court decided United States v. Haggar Apparel Co. (1999), holding that Customs regulations receive Chevron deference. The Federal Circuit asked for briefing on Haggar, then reversed, 185 F.3d 1304 (1999): ruling letters are not preceded by notice and comment, do not carry the force of law, and are not meant to fix importers' rights beyond the case at hand, so they get no deference at all. Deciding the question itself, the Federal Circuit held that planners are not diaries and that ring fastening is not "bound." The Supreme Court granted certiorari, 530 U.S. 1202 (2000), heard argument on November 8, 2000, and on June 18, 2001, vacated and remanded.
sections.Issue: Whether a tariff classification ruling letter issued by the Customs Service is entitled to deference under Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., so that a reviewing court must accept it if the statute is ambiguous and the ruling is reasonable; and, if Chevron does not apply, whether the ruling is owed any deference at all or, as the Federal Circuit held, none. Beneath that lies the framing question the Court took the case to answer: what indicates that Congress meant an agency to speak with the force of law when it interprets the statute it administers, and whether the answer turns on the procedure the agency used, the terms of the statutory grant, or simply whether the interpretation is the agency's authoritative position.
sections.Holding: "We hold that administrative implementation of a particular statutory provision qualifies for Chevron deference when it appears that Congress delegated authority to the agency generally to make rules carrying the force of law, and that the agency interpretation claiming deference was promulgated in the exercise of that authority." Such delegation may be shown by the agency's power to engage in adjudication or notice-and-comment rulemaking "or by some other indication of a comparable congressional intent." The Customs ruling letter fails that test: nothing in the statute or the agency's practice shows that Congress meant classification rulings to carry the force of law. But the letter is not owed no deference. Under Skidmore v. Swift & Co., it "is eligible to claim respect according to its persuasiveness." The judgment was vacated and the case remanded so the lower courts could make the Skidmore assessment in the first instance.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Souter began from a spectrum: courts weigh agency views by their care, consistency, formality, and expertness, as Skidmore said. Chevron identified a category with an added reason for deference, implicit delegation: when Congress would expect the agency to speak with the force of law, a court must accept a reasonable resolution of ambiguity. A very good indicator is an express authorization to engage in the rulemaking or adjudication that produces the ruling, and nearly all Chevron cases reviewed notice-and-comment rules or formal adjudications, though the absence of such procedure is not fatal (NationsBank). Here every angle pointed the same way. The statute authorizes "binding rulings" but nothing binding beyond the parties, and it provides for review on a fresh record in the Court of International Trade. Customs's practice disclaims third-party reliance and permits revocation without notice. The volume settles it: "Any suggestion that rulings intended to have the force of law are being churned out at a rate of 10,000 a year at an agency's 46 scattered offices is simply self-refuting." No statute treats Headquarters letters as a separate class. Classification rulings are like the policy statements and manuals of Christensen: "beyond the Chevron pale." Chevron did not abolish Skidmore, so an expert agency's ruling can still claim weight proportional to its thoroughness, logic, consistency, and fit with prior rulings. The Court chose to tailor deference to the variety of delegations rather than, as Scalia urged, to simplify.

topics.lrs-i-historical-chevron: Mead defined the threshold of the Chevron framework: deference applied only where Congress delegated force-of-law authority and the agency exercised it, typically through notice-and-comment rulemaking or formal adjudication.
topics.lrs-i-persuasive-weight: The Court held that Chevron left Skidmore intact, so an interpretation outside Chevron still earns respect proportional to its thoroughness, reasoning, consistency, and power to persuade; the remand was for exactly that assessment.
topics.lrs-i-delegated-discretion: The opinion lists the signals of a delegation to speak with the force of law, statutory grants of rulemaking or adjudicative power and agency practice that treats its output as binding, and finds none for 10,000 unpublished letters a year from 46 offices.
topics.lrs-n-guidance: Classification ruling letters were placed with the policy statements, manuals, and enforcement guidelines of Christensen v. Harris County: interpretive output that lacks the force of law and therefore cannot bind a reviewing court.
topics.lrs-i-independent-judgment: Scalia's dissent predicted ossification because a court's Skidmore reading becomes the statute's fixed meaning; after Loper Bright, that independent judicial reading, informed by Skidmore, is the rule for every agency interpretation.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 8 to 1. Justice Souter wrote for the Court, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer. Justice Scalia alone dissented, calling the decision "an avulsive change" that replaced Chevron's presumption of agency authority to resolve ambiguity with a presumption of no authority, resurrected Skidmore's "totality of the circumstances" test, and would produce confusion, an artificial rush to informal rulemaking ("Buy stock in the GPO"), and ossification, because once a court fixes a statute's meaning under Skidmore the agency can never change it. He argued that procedural formality has no logical connection to interpretive authority, that NationsBank, Philadelphia Gear, Young, and Mead v. Tilley had given Chevron deference to informal interpretations, and that the ruling here was the agency's authoritative position, vouched for by the Solicitor General and Treasury's General Counsel, reasonable, and therefore entitled to deference; he would have reversed and upheld the classification.
learning.why: Mead is the "step zero" case: it made Chevron turn on whether Congress delegated force-of-law authority and whether the agency used it, sorting rules, formal orders, guidance, and letters into different tiers. It also confirmed that Skidmore survived Chevron, which matters more now that Loper Bright has ended Chevron and left persuasive weight as the remaining form of respect for agency readings of statutes.
